real_s1.explanation: Within its preferred classes (mostly dogs and wild canids such as dingo, foxes and wolves, plus a few balls and an albatross), this unit's distinctive feature is a preference for subjects that face or point to the left. It is clearly more active for left-facing subjects than for right-facing ones (d about +0.9, 99th to 100th percentile in both photo sets, and the similar units do not share it). It is also more active for left-facing subjects than for subjects facing toward or away from the camera, and this held at the 98th percentile on the new photos. Frontal and directionless subjects fall in between. Their advantage over right-facing subjects did not reach the 95th-percentile threshold on new photos, so the effect is best described as a left-facing preference rather than a right-facing aversion. Warm tint, sharpness and subject size show weaker effects that are more ordinary for this layer.

real_s2.explanation: Within the same photo classes (mostly dogs and other canids), this unit is most active when the main subject faces or points left. It is lower for frontal or away-from-camera views and lowest for right-facing subjects. The left-over-right and left-over-frontal preferences replicated on new photos at the 98th to 99th percentile. Similar units do not share them, so this left-facing selectivity is what is particular to this unit. The apparent preference for warm-tinted photos did not replicate, and neither did the high response to photos with no clear facing direction. Framing, sharpness and lighting effects are typical for the layer.

real_s3.explanation: This unit responds to the direction the main subject faces. It is most active when the subject (usually a dog or other canid) faces or points to the left. It is less active when the subject faces the camera or away from it, and least active when the subject faces right. The left-over-right and left-over-frontal preferences are specific to this unit, since the similar units do not share them, and both held on new photos. The weaker preferences seen at first did not hold up: right-facing scoring below 'no clear direction' and warm tint scoring above no tint both failed on new photos.

null_s1.explanation: The unit responds mainly to its top classes: domestic dogs, wild canids such as dingo, foxes and wolves, and a few look-alikes like badger, Madagascar cat and balls. Within those classes, no property in the table is a reliable, unit-specific preference. The apparent dislike of right-facing subjects (rows 1, 2, 4, 5) did not replicate on 109 new photos. Left versus right fell from the 100th to the 65th percentile, and left versus frontal reversed sign. Only 'toward or away from the camera' over 'right' stayed fairly high (93rd, then 92nd percentile), and it never reached the 95th. The only other row at the 95th percentile or above is the mild warm-tint preference (row 13, 96th percentile), which was never checked on new photos. The size, cut-off and sharpness effects (rows 7–10, 19) are ordinary for this layer. So beyond class selectivity, nothing in the table can be confidently attributed to this unit.

null_s2.explanation: The unit's strongest drive is at the class level: dogs and other canids (dingo, corgis, foxes, wolves, hounds), plus a few other animals and balls. Within those classes, none of the annotated photo properties reliably explains its activity. The apparent preference for left-facing subjects over right-facing ones (rows 1, 2 and 5) and for warm-tinted photos (row 13) did not replicate on 109 new photos. All four rows fell to unremarkable or even reversed effects (percentiles 13 to 65). Framing, subject size, cut-off, position, lighting, tilt and sharpness effects were never unusual for this layer (all below 95). No row can be confidently said to describe something particular to this unit.

null_s3.explanation: The unit is most active on canids (dingo, foxes, wolves, many dog breeds) and a few other classes such as badger, albatross and rugby or soccer balls. Within those classes, none of the photo properties asked about reliably changes its activity. On the original photos, left-facing subjects seemed favored over right-facing ones and warm-tinted photos over untinted ones. All four picked rows (1, 5, 2, 13) fell to ordinary percentiles on new photos, and row 2 even reversed sign, so those effects look like noise. The rows that were not checked (pose, size, cropping, lighting, tint, tilt, sharpness) are all below the 95th percentile for this layer. So no row can be said to describe something particular to this unit.
